system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Literature search is not available in this session: judge novelty and mechanism from the data and your reasoning.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker MUT_ARID1A (damaging ARID1A mutation).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

name: scan_target

content.thinking: I've settled on ARID1B as the candidate, since its synthetic lethality is well established from the Helming 2014 and Kelso Nature work, so it's not a novel finding. I'll register it and set up the replication. One candidate is enough, so I'm registering it now.

input.mechanism: ARID1A and ARID1B are mutually exclusive paralogous subunits of the SWI/SNF (BAF) complex. Loss of ARID1A leaves cells reliant on ARID1B-containing BAF complexes for chromatin remodeling, so ARID1B knockout is selectively lethal in ARID1A-mutant cells while sparing ARID1A-intact cells (synthetic lethality via paralog buffering loss).

output: Registered H1_ARID1A_ARID1B: MUT_ARID1A -> more dependent on ARID1B. Discovery evidence frozen: t=-9.27, n_altered=57. Replication budget left: 5. Replication passes only if one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad lines and Sanger screens.

findings.claim: Cells with damaging ARID1A mutation depend selectively on ARID1B (SWI/SNF paralog): discovery beta -0.30 (t -9.3, 57 altered lines), held-out Broad beta -0.29 (p=2e-12), independent Sanger beta -0.17 (p=1e-5). Effect is weaker in Sanger and ARID1B is not broadly essential, supporting a selective window.

input.summary: Best candidate target for MUT_ARID1A tumours is ARID1B. It was the top lineage-adjusted dependency for MUT_ARID1A (q=6e-15), it is not broadly essential, and the signal was not driven by a single lineage (it held across uterus, ovary, bowel, breast). It replicated in held-out Broad lines (p=2e-12) and in independent Sanger screens (p=1e-5). This matches the known ARID1A/ARID1B paralog synthetic lethality, so the novelty is well established; the value here is the independent confirmation and the selectivity check. Weaker secondary signals (WRN, SIGLEC8, ARID2) were not pursued: they were less significant or were not clearly selective. Note the Sanger effect size is about half the Broad effect.
